analysis.one_liner: Lets people erase their personal data from every data broker with a single free request.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2022 with no cosponsors, referred to committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies that buy and sell people's personal information — data brokers, which trade in details about people they have no direct relationship with — to register with the Federal Trade Commission and disclose what they collect. It would then have created a free, government-run website where a person could make one request to have all registered data brokers delete their information within 31 days, and put that person on a do-not-track list so brokers could not restart collecting on them. The bill never advanced past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose information is bought and sold without their knowledge. Today, wiping your data means finding each broker separately and filing a separate request with each one; this bill would have replaced that with one free request that reaches every registered broker, including affiliates, and blocks them from collecting on you again. It also would have made brokers publicly disclose their data practices, giving people visibility into an industry most never see.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone tracked and sold by data brokers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a centralized FTC system where one submission triggers deletion of your personal information at every registered data broker and its affiliated entities.
Requires each broker to delete the matched information within 31 days and confirm to the FTC how many records it deleted.
Adds anyone who files a deletion request to a do-not-track list that bars registered brokers from collecting their personal information afterward.
Forces data brokers to register annually and disclose their data collection practices on a public, machine-readable FTC website.
The request is free to the individual, and violations are enforced by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the information-marketing businesses that profit from trading personal profiles, who would face registration, deletion, do-not-track, audit, and fee obligations. The FTC would run the system, funded by annual subscription fees charged to the registered brokers themselves.

drawbacks.text: The exemptions are broad: companies regulated under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, Gramm-Leach-Bliley, or HIPAA are not covered, so credit bureaus, banks, and health-data holders keep operating under older, weaker rules, and first-party tracking by companies you actually deal with is untouched.

To use the system, individuals must submit their email, phone number, physical address, and other persistent identifiers to an FTC-run registry; the bill requires strong security and automatic deletion after two years, but the government would still be assembling a national database of people most concerned about being tracked.

Enforcement rests entirely on FTC rulemaking and resources, and the system's funding comes from fees charged to the very brokers being regulated, which could be pressured or underfunded if few brokers register or comply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large for individuals: a one-stop, free escape hatch from an industry most people cannot even name, let alone negotiate with. The main weaknesses are scope, not principle — the exemptions leave much of the data economy out, and the security of a government-held identifier registry is a genuine but managed risk. On balance a well-aimed bill with practical rough edges.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, and the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lori Trahan introduced the DELETE Act in the House on February 15, 2022.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No cosponsors ever signed on, and the bill saw no further action of any kind before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the broader personal-data marketplace are better off: they kept selling and trading Americans' information with no registration requirement, no public disclosure of practices, and no deletion mechanism, and consumers remain on their own to chase each broker individually.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers, who kept selling unimpeded

for.name: Rep. Lori Trahan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; no colleagues signed on as cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Consumer Protection and Commerce Subcommittee and never took it up — no hearing, markup, or vote was held before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member publicly opposed the bill in the record; the closest signal is that it drew zero cosponsors from either party and died in a Democratic-controlled committee without action.

industries.note: These companies profit by collecting and selling personal information about people they have no direct relationship with. The bill would require them to register, disclose their practices, honor a single free deletion request within 31 days, stop collecting on requesters, pay fees, and submit to audits — cutting directly into their inventory and sales.
Targeting and list-building rely heavily on broker-sold profiles. Mass deletion requests and a do-not-track list would shrink the audience data available for ad targeting.
The bill requires every registered broker to undergo an independent audit every three years and keep records for six, creating paid compliance work.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus, banks, and health-data companies (FCRA/GLBA/HIPAA-regulated)
industries.note: Entities regulated under those older laws are explicitly excluded from the bill's definition of data broker, so their older, weaker rules stay in place and the bill's protections never reach them.
